title: The present subjunctive
topic: forming the subjunctive and its triggers
why: Here comes the subjunctive, the big project of level B1: the learner learns to form it (swapped vowel, stem from the yo form, six irregulars) and to use it after querer que, esperar que, ojalá, es importante que and para que. The lesson leads straight into choosing between subjunctive and indicative and expressing opinions.

Forming the subjunctive: swap the vowel

English barely has a subjunctive anymore (you'll find traces in “if I were you” or “I suggest that he be on time”), but Spanish uses it all the time. Think of it as a special verb form for things that are wished, needed or not yet real. Luckily, it's very regular: start from the yo form of the present, drop the -o, and use the vowel “of the other group”:

  • -ar verbs → endings in -e: habl-o → hable
  • -er and -ir verbs → endings in -a: com-o → coma, viv-o → viva
Personhablarcomervivir
(que) yohablecomaviva
(que) túhablescomasvivas
(que) él, ella, ustedhablecomaviva
(que) nosotros, nosotrashablemoscomamosvivamos
(que) vosotros, vosotrashabléiscomáisviváis
(que) ellos, ellas, ustedeshablencomanvivan

You've already seen these forms! The usted commands (hable, coma, siga) and the phrases perdone, disculpe are subjunctives. Note that the 1st and 3rd person singular are identical: que yo hable, que ella hable.

A few spelling changes

To keep the same sound, some verbs change a letter: llegar → llegue, buscar → busque, empezar → empiece, coger → coja.

", "

Irregular verbs

The stem of the yo form

Since you start from the yo form of the present, every verb that's irregular in the 1st person keeps that irregularity in all persons of the subjunctive:

Infinitiveyo (present)Subjunctive
tenertengotenga, tengas, tenga, tengamos, tengáis, tengan
hacerhagohaga, hagas, haga…
decirdigodiga, digas, diga…
salirsalgosalga, salgas, salga…
ponerpongoponga, pongas, ponga…
venirvengovenga, vengas, venga…
conocerconozcoconozca, conozcas, conozca…
oíroigooiga, oigas, oiga…

Stem-changing verbs keep their “boot” pattern, as in the present: pueda, puedas, pueda, podamos, podáis, puedan; quiera… queramos; entienda… entendamos (but dormir gives durmamos, durmáis). Verbs with e → i change everywhere: pida, pidas, pida, pidamos, pidáis, pidan.

The six truly irregular verbs

Personserirestarhabersaberdar
yoseavayaestéhayasepadé
túseasvayasestéshayassepasdes
él, ella, ustedseavayaestéhayasepadé
nosotrosseamosvayamosestemoshayamossepamosdemos
vosotrosseáisvayáisestéishayáissepáisdeis
ellos, ellas, ustedesseanvayanesténhayansepanden

Accents matter: esté, estés, estén; and dé (from dar) takes an accent so it isn't confused with the preposition de. Haya is the subjunctive of hay: Ojalá haya sitio. (I hope there's room.)

", "

When to use it: wishes and advice

The subjunctive appears after certain “triggers” followed by que. In this lesson: wanting, hoping, necessity and purpose.

TriggerExampleEnglish
querer queQuiero que vengas a la cena.I want you to come to the dinner.
esperar queEspero que estés bien.I hope you're well.
ojalá (que)¡Ojalá haga sol mañana!I really hope it's sunny tomorrow!
es importante queEs importante que descanses.It's important that you rest.
es mejor que, es necesario queEs mejor que vayamos en tren.It's better if we go by train.
para queTe lo explico para que lo entiendas.I'm explaining it so (that) you understand.

The big trap: English says “I want you to come” with an infinitive, but Spanish can't: it needs que + subjunctive. And “I hope you're well” uses a normal verb in English, but esperar que always takes the subjunctive in Spanish: Espero que estés bien, never “espero que estás bien.”

Only one subject? Use the infinitive

If the subject is the same in both parts of the sentence, keep the infinitive: Quiero ir (I want to go) but Quiero que vayas (I want you to go). Likewise, para + infinitive (same subject) / para que + subjunctive (different subjects).

Everyday wishes

Que + subjunctive on its own expresses a wish, a bit like English “May you…”. You'll hear these phrases everywhere in Spain: ¡Que aproveche! (Enjoy your meal!), ¡Que te mejores! (Get well soon!), ¡Que tengas buen día!, ¡Que lo paséis bien! (Have fun, all of you!), ¡Que tengas suerte!
